title: Find the Maximum Length of a Good Subsequence II
statement:
Call an integer sequence `seq` **good** if, read from left to right, its value switches at most `k` times: the number of positions `i` (`0 <= i <= seq.length - 2`) where `seq[i] != seq[i + 1]` is no more than `k`.

Given the integer array `nums` and the non-negative integer `k`, return the length of the longest good subsequence of `nums`. A subsequence keeps any selection of the elements (possibly all of them) in their original order.
notes:
## Intuition

A good subsequence is a chain of runs of equal values with at most `k` switches between runs. Trying every subsequence is exponential, and the usual table "longest chain ending at index `i` with at most `c` switches" checks every earlier index, which is O(n² · k): too slow for 5000 numbers.

Two observations remove the inner scan. To append `x` without a switch, only the best chain ending in the **value** `x` matters, not its index. To append `x` with a switch, any chain with one switch fewer will do, so only the overall best for each budget matters. So keep `dp[x][changes]` per value and `best[changes]` over all values.

## Approach

1. `dp` maps each value to a row of `k + 1` lengths, all starting at 0; `best` has one entry per budget.
2. For each `x` in `nums`, go through the budgets `changes` from `k` **down** to 0:
   - append `x` to the best chain already ending in `x` (no switch): `row[changes] + 1`;
   - or, if `changes > 0`, append it to the best chain with one switch fewer: `best[changes - 1] + 1`;
   - raise `best[changes]` to the new value.
3. Return `best[k]`.

Going downward means `best[changes - 1]` has not yet been raised by the current element, so no element is used twice. If the best chain with one switch fewer already ends in `x`, appending `x` costs no switch at all, so the value is still reachable.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 1, 1, 3]`, `k = 2`. Rows are budgets 0 to 2:

- `1`: `dp[1] = [1, 1, 1]`, `best = [1, 1, 1]`.
- `2`: `dp[2] = [1, 2, 2]`, `best = [1, 2, 2]`.
- `1`: `dp[1] = [2, 2, 3]` (budget 2 extends `best[1] = 2`), `best = [2, 2, 3]`.
- `1`: `dp[1] = [3, 3, 4]`, `best = [3, 3, 4]`.
- `3`: `dp[3] = [1, 4, 4]`, `best = [3, 4, 4]`.

The answer is `best[2] = 4`, for example `[1, 2, 1, 1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · k): constant work per element and budget.
- Space: O(d · k) for `d` distinct values (at most `n`).

## Pitfalls

- Looping `changes` upward lets `best[changes - 1]` already contain the current element, which then counts twice.
- Values reach 10^9, so index the table by a `Map` (or compressed values), not by the value itself.
- The budget means "at most `k`" switches, so the answer is `best[k]`, not a maximum over exact counts.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp` | for each value `x`, its row of lengths |
| `row[changes]` | longest good subsequence ending in value `x` with at most `changes` switches |
| `best[changes]` | longest good subsequence so far, any last value, at most `changes` switches |
| `x` | the current element of `nums` |
| `changes` | the switch budget being updated |

narration.2: dp maps each value to its row: the longest good subsequence ending in that value, for every switch budget.
narration.3: best[changes] is the longest good subsequence so far with at most changes switches, whatever its last value.
narration.5: Take the elements in order; each one may extend subsequences built from earlier elements.
narration.6: The first time a value appears it has no chains yet...
narration.7: ...so give it a row of zeros.
narration.9: row is the table entry for the current value x.
narration.10: Go through the budgets from k down to 0, so best[changes - 1] still describes earlier elements only.
narration.11: Append x to the best chain already ending in x: equal neighbours need no switch.
narration.12: With at least one switch to spend...
narration.13: ...x may instead follow the best chain that used one switch fewer, whatever value it ends in.
narration.15: Raise the overall best for this budget.
narration.18: Return the longest good subsequence with at most k switches.
